newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Developing countries oppose WTO investment role.
newsitem.headline: Developing countries oppose WTO investment role.

text.p: Eight developing countries have written the head of the World Trade Organisation (WTO) urging that the controversial question of rules on foreign investment not be discussed by ministers meeting in Singapore next month.

In a letter to WTO director-general Renato Ruggiero they argued that the U.N. Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD) was the appropriate forum for studying the link between trade and investment.

The European Union, Japan and Canada -- three of the four top world trade powers -- are pushing hard for the investment issue to be included in the Singapore ministerial declaration, which would set out a WTO work programme for the next two years.
The three-page text, obtained by Reuters, was sent on Wednesday by Egypt, Ghana, Haiti, India, Indonesia, Malaysia, Tanzania and Uganda.
"The first WTO ministerial conference is not an appropriate occasion for introducing the issue of trade and investment," the joint letter said.
"Attempts to do so would be contentious, and would distract and detract from the many important items already on the agenda," it said, warning of "undesirable spillover effects".

"It is obvious that there is no consensus in the WTO on this issue...Given the lack of consensus, we urge there should not be any further consideration of this issue within the WTO, until the processes envisaged in UNCTAD is sufficiently mature."

The eight countries said that introducing new issues on the agenda of the WTO, which succeded the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT) less than two years ago, would overload the new structure and put "great strain" on delegations.

"We are therefore of the view that any review of the adequacy of the treatment of trade and investment in the WTO should take place only in the course of the review of the Trade- Related Investment Measures (TRIMS) at the appropriate time," they said, referring to the TRIMS pact under the Uruguay Round.

Other controversial issues which major powers have been seeking to put on the Singapore agenda -- against fierce opposition from developing countries -- including labour standards, corruption and competition policy.
